blocks.en: Unit Five · Stage 3: Develop the Sermon
blocks.es_reference: Unidad Cinco · Etapa 3: Desarrollar el Sermón

blocks.en: Amplify the Outline
blocks.es_reference: Amplificar el Bosquejo

blocks.en: EAI — explanation, application, illustration — plus four alternative methods for developing each division.
blocks.es_reference: EAI — explicación, aplicación, ilustración — más cuatro métodos alternativos para desarrollar cada división.

blocks.en: 5.1 The EAI Method
blocks.es_reference: 5.1 El Método EAI

blocks.en: One of the simplest ways of developing the sermon after completing the outline is to use explanation, application, and illustration for each division. For purposes of this course we will call this the EAI Method. The order of these three elements may vary — you may start with illustration, proceed with application, and conclude with explanation. The same procedure is used for every point until the sermon is finished. Each of the three parts would normally receive the same attention, although they may not be exactly the same length. Repeat the procedure for topical, textual, or expository messages.
blocks.es_reference: Una de las formas más simples de desarrollar el sermón después de completar el bosquejo es usar explicación, aplicación e ilustración para cada división. Para los propósitos de este curso lo llamaremos el Método EAI. El orden de estos tres elementos puede variar — puede comenzar con la ilustración, proceder con la aplicación y concluir con la explicación. El mismo procedimiento se usa para cada punto hasta que el sermón se termine. Cada una de las tres partes normalmente recibiría la misma atención, aunque no necesariamente la misma longitud exacta. Repita el procedimiento para mensajes temáticos, textuales o expositivos.

blocks.en: 5.2 Explanation
blocks.es_reference: 5.2 Explicación

blocks.en: Explanation means "to bring out the meaning, to make plain, to make clear." This may take several different forms. (1) Explaining the meaning of the text — the interpreter asks, "What exactly was the Biblical writer saying to his hearers?" Here one seeks to draw out and explain the meaning of the text. (2) Narration — one gives the bare account of an event. You might tell the story of a Biblical character such as Daniel or Abraham. (3) Description — you describe how something appears to the five senses. You are painting a picture with words.
blocks.es_reference: Explicación significa "sacar el significado, aclarar, hacer claro." Esto puede tomar varias formas diferentes. (1) Explicar el significado del texto — el intérprete pregunta: "¿Qué exactamente estaba diciendo el escritor bíblico a sus oyentes?" Aquí uno busca extraer y explicar el significado del texto. (2) Narración — uno da el relato simple de un evento. Podría contar la historia de un personaje bíblico como Daniel o Abraham. (3) Descripción — usted describe cómo algo aparece a los cinco sentidos. Está pintando un cuadro con palabras.

blocks.en: 5.3 Application — Master of All
blocks.es_reference: 5.3 Aplicación — La Maestra de Todo

blocks.en: Application is the master of all whereas the illustration is the servant of all. Charles H. Spurgeon said that application is where the sermon actually begins. It seeks to relate Biblical truth to people's lives. Otherwise it is just an historical Bible study. While there may be some value in such a study, it will not have much of an impact upon people's lives. Harry Emerson Fosdick said that people are not interested in what God said to the Jebusites. They are interested in what God is saying to them today through the story of the Jebusites.
blocks.es_reference: La aplicación es la maestra de todo, mientras que la ilustración es la sierva de todo. Charles H. Spurgeon dijo que la aplicación es donde el sermón realmente comienza. Busca relacionar la verdad bíblica con las vidas de las personas. De lo contrario es solo un estudio bíblico histórico. Aunque puede haber algún valor en tal estudio, no tendrá mucho impacto sobre las vidas de las personas. Harry Emerson Fosdick dijo que las personas no están interesadas en lo que Dios dijo a los jebuseos. Están interesadas en lo que Dios les está diciendo hoy a través de la historia de los jebuseos.

blocks.en: Research suggests that unless the application is made by the speaker, it will not be made by the hearers. Application should be very personal — use "we" in speaking and answer "What should we do?" It should be in the present tense and should answer "What should we do right now?" It should be dynamic and changing — the truths of Scripture do not change, but applications of these truths do change with the times. It should suggest ways and means — "How are we to put this into practice today?"
blocks.es_reference: La aplicación es la maestra de todo, mientras que la ilustración es la sierva de todo. Charles H. Spurgeon dijo que la aplicación es donde el sermón realmente comienza. Busca relacionar la verdad bíblica con las vidas de las personas. De lo contrario es solo un estudio bíblico histórico. Aunque puede haber algún valor en tal estudio, no tendrá mucho impacto sobre las vidas de las personas. Harry Emerson Fosdick dijo que las personas no están interesadas en lo que Dios dijo a los jebuseos. Están interesadas en lo que Dios les está diciendo hoy a través de la historia de los jebuseos.

blocks.en: Show model: Then / Universal / Now method
blocks.es_reference: Mostrar modelo: método Entonces / Universal / Ahora

blocks.en: Three steps to make an application:
blocks.es_reference: Tres pasos para hacer una aplicación:

blocks.en:
(1) Then — what the text said to its original hearers.
(2) Universal — the timeless principle that transcends culture.
(3) Now — the specific application for today.

Example:
#1 Then. Jesus calmed the storm on the Sea of Galilee, and the storm in the lives of the disciples (Matthew 8:24-27).
#2 Universal. Jesus has the power to calm outer and inner storms that rage in people's lives.
#3 Now. Jesus calms outer and inner storms today such as loneliness, sickness, fear, and anxiety.
blocks.es_reference:
(1) Entonces — lo que el texto dijo a sus oyentes originales.
(2) Universal — el principio atemporal que trasciende la cultura.
(3) Ahora — la aplicación específica para hoy.

Ejemplo:
#1 Entonces. Jesús calmó la tormenta en el mar de Galilea, y la tormenta en las vidas de los discípulos (Mateo 8:24-27).
#2 Universal. Jesús tiene el poder de calmar tormentas externas e internas que rugen en las vidas de las personas.
#3 Ahora. Jesús calma tormentas externas e internas hoy tales como soledad, enfermedad, miedo y ansiedad.

blocks.en: 5.4 Illustration — Servant of All
blocks.es_reference: 5.4 Ilustración — La Sierva de Todo

blocks.en: No book is completely adequate for producing illustrations. The word "illustrate" means to throw light upon. A human interest story makes the sermon come alive. Try for at least one good illustration per division — every point you make should be illustrated. I usually also use one in the introduction and one in the conclusion. Many students and pastors report that the finding of good illustrations is the most difficult task they face.
blocks.es_reference: Ningún libro es completamente adecuado para producir ilustraciones. La palabra "ilustrar" significa arrojar luz sobre. Una historia de interés humano hace que el sermón cobre vida. Procure al menos una buena ilustración por división — cada punto que haga debe ser ilustrado. Usualmente también uso una en la introducción y una en la conclusión. Muchos estudiantes y pastores reportan que encontrar buenas ilustraciones es la tarea más difícil que enfrentan.

blocks.en: Six sources of illustrations: (1) The Bible itself — biographies, parables, figures, or historical events. When you do this, the congregation may not know you are illustrating; you have the advantage of teaching the Bible at the same time. (2) Observation — keep a notebook of observations from nature, science, psychology, and people. Be discreet about using examples of church members or family. (3) Newspapers, newscasts, and news magazines — current events make Scripture feel immediate. (4) General reading and viewing — history, literature, films, novels. (5) Pastoral work — visits often produce illustrations; sometimes ask permission to share a story. (6) Personal experience — a form of testimony where you tell about something that happened to you.
blocks.es_reference: Ningún libro es completamente adecuado para producir ilustraciones. La palabra "ilustrar" significa arrojar luz sobre. Una historia de interés humano hace que el sermón cobre vida. Procure al menos una buena ilustración por división — cada punto que haga debe ser ilustrado. Usualmente también uso una en la introducción y una en la conclusión. Muchos estudiantes y pastores reportan que encontrar buenas ilustraciones es la tarea más difícil que enfrentan.

blocks.en: 5.5 Additional Subdivision Methodologies
blocks.es_reference: 5.5 Metodologías Adicionales de Subdivisión

blocks.en: Apart from EAI there are several other methods for forming subpoints. With any of these the subpoints should appear in the preacher's notes but should very rarely be stated while delivering the sermon. Because preaching is an oral art form, too many subpoints are confusing rather than enlightening.
blocks.es_reference: 1. El método de palabra clave. Una palabra clave se usa al formar las subdivisiones de la misma manera que una palabra clave enlaza las divisiones principales. Cada división podría ser realmente un segundo sermón. Job 1:1 y Job 21:7 producen dos grandes preguntas: "¿Por qué sufren los buenos?" (subdivisiones con palabra clave resultados positivos: Job aprendió de su orgullo, de la paciencia, de la providencia de Dios) y "¿Por qué prosperan los impíos?" (subdivisiones con palabra clave razones: las cosas no son siempre como parecen; la paciencia y misericordia de Dios; un día Dios pondrá todas las cosas en orden).

blocks.en: 1. The keyword method. A keyword is used in forming the subdivisions the same way a keyword links the main divisions. Each division could actually be a second sermon. Job 1:1 and Job 21:7 yield two great questions: "Why do the good suffer?" (subdivisions named with keyword positive results: Job learned of his pride, of patience, of God's providence) and "Why do the wicked prosper?" (subdivisions named with keyword reasons: things are not always as they appear; God's patience and mercy; one day God will make all things right).

Cada división podría ser realmente un segundo sermón. Job 1:1 y Job 21:7 producen dos grandes preguntas: "¿Por qué sufren los buenos?" (subdivisiones con palabra clave resultados positivos: Job aprendió de su orgullo, de la paciencia, de la providencia de Dios) y "¿Por qué prosperan los impíos?" (subdivisiones con palabra clave razones: las cosas no son siempre como parecen; la paciencia y misericordia de Dios; un día Dios pondrá todas las cosas en orden).

blocks.en: 2. The series of statements method. No attempt is made to discover a keyword for the subdivisions. The statements are rapid-fire concepts designed to provoke thought and stimulate word pictures. Mark 5:25-34, "He Touched Me" — Subject = Areas Jesus made the woman whole. Under "Christ made her physically whole" you might list: She had a foolish faith / She had an ignorant faith / She had a genuine faith. The healing was free; it was immediate.

blocks.en: 3. The combination method. Combine several methods, using one for one division and another for the next. The explanation method might be used for one point and the series of statements or keyword method for others.

blocks.en: 4. EAI revisited. Return to EAI when the unit's content calls for substantial development on a single point — explanation drawn from the text, application drawn from the universal-to-now bridge, illustration drawn from any of the six sources above.

mc.stem: What does Wayne call the primary subdivision method introduced in Unit 5?
mc.why: EAI = Explanation, Application, Illustration — Wayne's name for the primary subpoint development method.

mc.stem: Wayne lists three forms of explanation. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Explaining the meaning of the text
mc.why: The three forms are explaining the meaning, narration, and description. Memorization is a delivery method, not an explanation form.

mc.stem: Wayne says application is the master of all whereas the illustration is the:
mc.why: Application is master; illustration is servant. The illustration serves the application, not the other way around.

mc.stem: Which preacher did Wayne quote as saying that application is where the sermon actually begins?
mc.why: Spurgeon said the sermon actually begins with application.

mc.stem: Harry Emerson Fosdick said people are not interested in what God said to the:
mc.why: Fosdick: 'They are interested in what God is saying to them today through the story of the Jebusites.'

mc.stem: Wayne's three-step method for making an application is:
mc.why: Then (what the text said originally) → Universal (the timeless principle) → Now (the specific application today).

mc.stem: Application characteristics include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Present tense ('what should we do right now?')
mc.why: Application MUST be personal. The other three characteristics are required; this one inverts the principle.

mc.stem: What does the word 'illustrate' literally mean?
mc.why: 'Illustrate' literally means to throw light upon. The illustration sheds light on the truth being preached.

mc.stem: How often does Wayne recommend illustrating in a sermon?
options: At least one good illustration per division, plus one in the introduction and conclusion
Only when the audience seems bored
mc.why: At least one per division, plus one in the introduction and one in the conclusion.

mc.stem: Wayne lists six sources of illustrations. Which is NOT one of them?
mc.why: The six sources are Bible, observation, news, general reading/viewing, pastoral work, and personal experience. Commentaries belong to study, not to illustration.

mc.stem: What advantage does the Bible-as-illustration source have, according to Wayne?
options: The congregation may not know you are illustrating — you are also teaching the Bible at the same time
It avoids the need for application
It frees you from preparing the sermon
It impresses scholars in the audience
mc.why: Biblical illustrations teach the Bible while illustrating — a double yield.

mc.stem: Apart from EAI, what is the 'keyword method' of forming subdivisions?
options: Using a keyword to organize the subpoints the way one organizes the main divisions
Naming each point with a keyword from a hymn
Using only nouns starting with the same letter
mc.why: The keyword method uses a keyword inside the subdivision the same way a keyword links the main divisions.

mc.stem: Wayne cautions about subpoints in general:
options: They should appear in the preacher's notes but rarely be stated aloud — preaching is oral, and too many subpoints confuse rather than enlighten
They must always be announced aloud
They should outnumber the main divisions
They are required by every sermon
mc.why: Subpoints structure the preacher's thinking but should rarely be announced; preaching is oral.

mc.stem: In the 'series of statements' subdivision method:
options: Each subdivision must have a Bible reference
No keyword is used; rapid-fire statements provoke thought and paint word pictures
Subdivisions must all begin with the same letter
Each statement must be a full paragraph
mc.why: Series of statements — no keyword, just rapid concepts designed to stimulate word pictures.

mc.stem: Wayne's 'combination method' for subdivisions means:
options: Mixing English and Spanish in the outline
Combining two different sermons into one
Using different subdivision methods for different divisions in the same sermon
Combining text and topic into one outline
mc.why: You may use EAI for one division, keyword method for another, series for a third — fit the method to each point.

mc.stem: The three letters of the EAI method stand for:
mc.why: EAI = Explanation, Application, Illustration — written for each main division.

mc.stem: The course says that unless the application is made by the speaker, it will:
options: Not be made by the hearers
mc.why: Research suggests the hearers will not apply it unless the speaker does it for them.

mc.stem: The Then / Universal / Now method is mainly a tool for which part of EAI?
mc.why: It bridges the ancient text to the modern hearer — the work of application.

mc.stem: The word 'illustrate' literally means:
mc.why: To illustrate is to throw light upon — making the truth clear and vivid.

mc.stem: Wayne calls the illustration 'the servant of all,' which warns against letting it become:
mc.why: When the story becomes master, the sermon collapses into entertainment with weak Bible.

sa.prompt: Explain the EAI method of developing subdivisions. Why does Wayne say that EAI is the simplest way to develop a sermon after completing the outline?
sa.model: EAI = Explanation, Application, Illustration. For each main division you write the explanation, the application, and the illustration; repeat for every point. Wayne calls it simplest because (1) it provides a default template that works for topical, textual, and expository sermons; (2) it forces the preacher to provide all three elements rather than skipping any; (3) it gives the congregation a predictable rhythm — they know each point will be explained, applied, and illustrated. The order of E, A, I can vary, but the three elements must all be present.

sa.prompt: List Wayne's three forms of explanation and give an example of when each would be most appropriate.
sa.model: (1) Explaining the meaning of the text: the interpreter asks, "What exactly was the Biblical writer saying to his hearers?" and draws out and explains the meaning; appropriate when the point is to make the writer's message plain. (2) Narration: the bare account of an event, such as the story of a Biblical character like Daniel or Abraham; appropriate when the account itself carries the truth. (3) Description: telling how something appears to the five senses, painting a picture with words; appropriate when the hearers need to see the scene.

sa.prompt: Walk through the Then / Universal / Now method using a passage Wayne does NOT supply in the unit. Show how you would move from the original cultural setting to a timeless principle to a current application.
sa.model: Strong answers pick a passage with clear cultural distance. Example for Acts 10 (Peter and the Gentile Cornelius): Then — Peter was told God had cleansed what tradition called unclean, breaking the Jew/Gentile food and fellowship divide. Universal — God breaks down barriers that human tradition treats as sacred when those barriers exclude people He has accepted. Now — congregations today need to examine their own unspoken admission criteria (class, ethnicity, dress, marriage history) and confess any tradition that excludes those God has cleansed. The strong answer also notes Wayne's caution: many applications of one universal are possible, and the preacher chooses the most pressing for his hearers.

sa.prompt: Why does Wayne insist that application must be made by the speaker rather than left for the listeners to infer? Cite the research finding he references and give two practical implications.
sa.model: Research suggests that unless the application is made by the speaker, it will not be made by the hearers. Implications: (1) The sermon must include explicit 'so what?' language — 'we should…', 'this means…', 'this requires…' — not just exposition. (2) Application should appear in multiple places (introduction, with each point, in the conclusion), not buried in one paragraph at the end. (3) Wayne's preference for the present tense ('what should we do right now?') reinforces that the listener should leave knowing exactly what to do this week, not someday. Strong answers note that this is also why pure exposition without application — however accurate — fails as preaching.

sa.prompt: Identify and briefly describe at least four of Wayne's six sources of illustrations.
sa.model: (1) The Bible itself: biographies, parables, figures, or historical events; the congregation may not know you are illustrating, and you teach the Bible at the same time. (2) Observation: keep a notebook of observations from nature, science, psychology, and people; be discreet about using examples of church members or family. (3) Newspapers, newscasts, and news magazines: current events make Scripture feel immediate. (4) General reading and viewing: history, literature, films, novels. (5) Pastoral work: visits often produce illustrations; sometimes ask permission to share a story. (6) Personal experience: a form of testimony in which you tell about something that happened to you.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between the keyword subdivision method and the series-of-statements method. When is each most useful?
sa.model: Keyword method: a keyword is used to organize the subpoints inside each division the same way a keyword links the main divisions. Best when each main division has multiple parallel sub-claims that share a common category — e.g., 'reasons' or 'evidences.' Series of statements: no keyword is sought; rapid, parallel statements designed to provoke thought and paint pictures. Best when the preacher wants emotional and cumulative force — telling, not categorizing — as in the 'He Touched Me' sermon where each subpoint is an imaginative statement ('imagine her loneliness, imagine her despair…'). Wayne notes that the keyword method can be tedious for listeners since it asks them to hold multiple categorized lists in mind at once; the series-of-statements method moves faster but sacrifices structure.

sa.prompt: Take an outline you have developed earlier in this course and write out a sketchy EAI development of one of its points. Show clearly which sentences are explanation, which are application, and which are illustration.
sa.model: Strong answer shows a labeled three-part development. Example using the Psalm 103 outline from Unit 4, point I ("Because God forgives us," v. 3a). Explanation: "The Psalmist is praising God for His goodness, and the first reason he gives is that God forgives; David is telling his own soul that God pardons all our iniquities." Application: "We should stop carrying the guilt God has already forgiven. What should we do right now? We should confess what is on our conscience today and receive His forgiveness as settled." Illustration (from the Bible itself, one of the six sources): "In Jesus' parable of the prodigal son, the father does not make his son earn his way back; he runs down the road and embraces him. That is a picture of how God forgives." The three parts receive roughly equal attention.

sa.prompt: Wayne calls illustrations 'the servant of all.' What danger arises when illustration becomes the master instead, and how does the preacher avoid that danger while still making generous use of illustrations?
sa.model: Application is the master of all, whereas the illustration is the servant of all. The illustration exists to throw light upon the point; a human interest story makes the sermon come alive. When it becomes the master, it takes the place of application, which Spurgeon said is where the sermon actually begins, and the sermon stops relating Biblical truth to people's lives. It becomes an historical study with stories attached, and the people may remember the story but not what the truth means for them. The preacher avoids this by keeping the illustration in its place, one good illustration per division (and one in the introduction and the conclusion) to make every point come alive, while the speaker himself makes the application, personal, in the present tense, answering "What should we do right now?"

sa.prompt: Walk through the full EAI development of ONE point of an outline of your choosing. Label the Explanation, the Application, and the Illustration clearly, and make sure the application names a concrete action.
sa.model: Strong answer shows a clearly labeled three-part development on one chosen point: Explanation (what the text means), Application (a concrete 'relevance' the hearer must do — not just a belief), and Illustration (a story or image that throws light on the point). The application must be made by the speaker and name an action.

sa.prompt: Name four of the six sources of illustrations the course gives. For two of them, state the advantage or the caution the course attaches to it.
sa.model: Strong answer names four of the six sources (the Bible itself, observation, newspapers and news magazines, general reading and viewing, pastoral work, personal experience) and, for two, gives what the course says: the Bible is an advantage because the congregation may not know you are illustrating and you teach the Bible at the same time; observation calls for a notebook, and the caution to be discreet about using examples of church members or family; pastoral work often produces illustrations, but sometimes ask permission to share a story.
